rule: When a service option lets the user pick a combination of values, expose it as a `select` selector with `multiple: true` rather than inventing a synthetic combined option such as `both`, matching the selector shape sibling integrations already use for the same service.
trigger: A `services.yaml` diff adds or edits a `select` selector whose `options` list contains an aggregate value (`both`, `all`, `any`) alongside the individual values.
rationale: Reviewers point at the equivalent service in another integration (Nordpool's `get_prices_for_date`) and expect the same selector shape; `multiple: true` is the platform-supported way to express a combination, so the extra option is redundant UI and diverges from the established service schema.

evidence.excerpt: uses for the same get_prices_for_date service a select that allows multiple options

rule: Exception and issue messages in `strings.json` that reuse text defined elsewhere must point at it with an exact `[%key:component::<domain>::<section>::<key>%]` reference, with no stray whitespace inside the reference path.
trigger: A `strings.json` diff adds a message whose value is a `[%key:...%]` reference, or duplicates a message string already defined under `config`/`exceptions` in the same file.
rationale: The `[%key:...%]` indirection is how the repo keeps one wording for one concept across config flow aborts and runtime exceptions; the reference is resolved by exact string match, so a single stray space silently breaks the link to the existing string.

evidence.excerpt: removing the stray space so it correctly points at the existing config.abort.connection_error string

rule: Name a module-level tuple of `EntityDescription` objects after the platform it populates (`SENSOR_DESCRIPTIONS`, `SELECT_TYPES`), not after one entity or one subset of the entities it contains.
trigger: A platform module (`sensor.py`, `select.py`, ...) declares a `tuple[...EntityDescription, ...]` constant, or a diff adds descriptions to an existing one so the constant now covers more than its name implies.
rationale: These tuples are the dispatch table the platform iterates over during `async_setup_entry`; a name describing only one member misleads the next contributor adding a description and makes the entity set look narrower than it is.

evidence.excerpt: constant name is misleading; renaming to SENSOR_DESCRIPTIONS/QUOTA_SENSORS would make the intent clearer

rule: Diagnostics collectors must only read known-safe attributes of the device/client object and must never invoke callables found on it.
trigger: `diagnostics.py` walks attributes of a client/device object and calls anything it finds callable (`if callable(val): val = val()`), or uses `hasattr()` followed by `getattr()` to probe for attributes.
rationale: Downloading diagnostics is a user-triggered read-only operation; calling arbitrary methods on the library object can perform I/O, mutate device state, or emit huge unstable payloads, and attribute probing can fire `__getattr__` side effects.

evidence.excerpt: calling a method during diagnostics can trigger I/O, mutate device state, or produce large/unstable output

rule: Build the diagnostics payload by dumping the coordinator/client data directly into a dict; do not add a generic recursive JSON-coercion layer that walks arbitrary object graphs.
trigger: `diagnostics.py` adds a helper that recursively coerces arbitrary values (lists/dicts/sets/enums/callables) into JSON-safe values, with depth limits or type fallbacks.
rationale: Reviewers question why integration data would ever be complex enough to need it: the library payload is expected to be dict-shaped already, and a bespoke serializer is untested surface area sitting in the diagnostics path.

evidence.excerpt: do we really expect the data to be this complex

rule: Production integration code must not detect or branch on test doubles; fix the fixture or the test instead of adding mock-aware code paths under `homeassistant/components/`.
trigger: A file under `homeassistant/components/` references `mock_add_spec`, `unittest.mock`, `MagicMock`, or otherwise special-cases behaviour when the object appears to be a mock.
rationale: Sniffing for mock internals is a brittle implementation detail that can be true for non-mock objects, and it bakes the shape of the test suite into shipped integration code.

rule: Diagnostics output must be deterministic: never emit values rendered through a default `repr`/`str` that embeds memory addresses or other run-specific detail; use a stable representation such as the type name or `__qualname__`.
trigger: `diagnostics.py` formats an unknown object into the payload via an f-string or `str()` fallback (`f"<{type(k).__name__}: {k}>"`) for keys or values of arbitrary type.
rationale: Diagnostics payloads are asserted against stored snapshots, so any address- or identity-dependent text makes the snapshot test flap and makes user-submitted logs impossible to diff.

evidence.excerpt: This undermines deterministic diagnostics output and makes tests/logs brittle

rule: During `async_setup_entry`, configure the library client so connection and auth exceptions propagate instead of being swallowed by a client-side "suppress errors" mode, so setup can raise `ConfigEntryNotReady`/auth failure; keep the suppressing mode for the post-setup refresh loop only.
trigger: `__init__.py` constructs the integration's API client for setup with a flag (e.g. `initial=True`) that suppresses or only logs exceptions, then wraps the first call in try/except.
rationale: If the client eats the first connection error, setup succeeds against an unreachable device and the user gets a config entry that can never work rather than a retrying `ConfigEntryNotReady`; the same reasoning applies to the config flow, which should validate with a throwaway client.

evidence.excerpt: It surpresses exceptions which we would rather catch here I think

rule: A workaround that overrides entity `available` (or any other device-quirk fallback) must ship a regression test covering both the workaround path and the genuine-failure path, asserting real unavailable events still mark the entity unavailable.
trigger: `entity.py` overrides the `available` property with device- or API-type-specific special casing (e.g. only for `APIType.LOCAL`) and the PR adds no matching test.
rationale: Availability workarounds silently mask upstream bugs; without a test pinning both directions, a later refactor either drops the fallback or leaves entities permanently available when the device really is offline.

evidence.excerpt: Add a regression test covering the new local-API availability fallback

rule: Config-flow credential validation that iterates a listing endpoint must treat an empty result as a validation failure (set `errors["base"]`) rather than creating the entry, and `async_setup_entry` must apply the same check.
trigger: `config_flow.py` validates the connection by iterating an API listing (`async for _ in client.models.list(): break`) and only treats raised exceptions as failure.
rationale: Some APIs return an empty iterator instead of raising for a bad key, so the flow otherwise happily creates a config entry that can never work; the flow and setup must agree on what counts as a working connection.

evidence.excerpt: Treat an empty iterator as a failed validation (e.g., set errors["base"] = "cannot_connect")

rule: `quality_scale.yaml` exemption comments must not contradict `manifest.json`; if a rule is marked exempt because the integration "does not poll", the manifest `iot_class` must agree (or the comment must state precisely what it does instead).
trigger: A PR adds or edits `quality_scale.yaml` entries with `status: exempt` and a justification comment about polling, actions, or discovery that conflicts with the integration's `manifest.json`.
rationale: The quality scale file is the reviewed record of an integration's obligations; a justification that contradicts the declared `iot_class` means one of the two is wrong and the exemption cannot be trusted.

evidence.excerpt: This states the integration 'does not poll', but the integration metadata sets iot_class to cloud_polling

rule: Import a library's exception classes from one module path consistently across the integration and its tests, and confirm that path is actually exported by the version pinned in `manifest.json`.
trigger: A PR bumps a library and adds imports of its exception types, with the integration importing from the package root while the tests import the same names from a submodule (or vice versa).
rationale: Package-level re-exports are not guaranteed by the pinned version, so a split import means the integration can fail at import time while the tests pass against the submodule path the library really exposes.

evidence.excerpt: Verify that these exceptions are exported at the package level in python-picnic-api2 v1.3.4

rule: A `deprecated_yaml` repair issue description must name the concrete legacy action/service names the user actually has (e.g. `tts.picotts_say`), not a templated glob like `tts.{domain}_*_say`.
trigger: `strings.json` adds an `issues.deprecated_yaml` description that refers to the services being removed with a wildcard or placeholder pattern.
rationale: The repair issue is the migration instruction the user follows; the legacy platform registers a specific default service name (and users may have overridden it), so a pattern leaves them guessing which automations to update.

evidence.excerpt: Consider rewording this to mention the actual legacy service name(s) to avoid confusing users

rule: A dependency-bump PR must contain only the changes required by the version update; new user-facing entities, platforms, or features belong in a separate feature PR.
trigger: A PR whose stated purpose is bumping a library version also adds entity descriptions, dispatch entries, constants, fixtures, and tests for a new entity.
rationale: Bump PRs are reviewed and released on a different track from features; mixing a new Select entity into one hides a user-facing change behind a compatibility label and makes the bump hard to revert.

evidence.excerpt: dependency-bump PRs must remain limited to changes required for the version update

rule: When an integration runs more than one `DataUpdateCoordinator`, give each a distinct `name` (e.g. `f"{DOMAIN}_{self.__class__.__name__}"`) rather than passing `DOMAIN` to all of them.
trigger: `coordinator.py` adds a second coordinator subclass whose `super().__init__()` passes the same `name=DOMAIN` as the existing coordinator.
rationale: `DataUpdateCoordinator` puts `name` into every debug/error log line and update-failure message; identical names make it impossible to tell which refresh loop failed.

evidence.excerpt: Give the slow coordinator a distinct `name` from the main coordinator

rule: A coordinator that fans out over several devices/endpoints must fetch them concurrently (`asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True)`) and isolate per-item failures, keeping previous values for the ones that error instead of failing the whole refresh.
trigger: `_async_update_data` awaits an API call inside a `for` loop over endpoints/devices, letting the first exception abort the whole update.
rationale: Sequential awaits serialise every device's latency, and one slow or failing endpoint marks every entity from every other endpoint unavailable.

evidence.excerpt: one slow/failing endpoint does not fail the entire disk-space refresh
